name: Nikhil Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Nikhil. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a five-person agency that makes online ads for small web shops: a plant shop, a tea company, a guy who resells trainers. Most days I'm turning one product photo into thirty ad versions for different sites and screen sizes. I use AI tools all day, for background swaps, first drafts of layouts and testing which headline gets more clicks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can see results the same afternoon: change a colour, and the click rate moves. What wears me out is the speed, because a web shop wants new ads every week, and it never stops. Sam, who co-founded the agency, calls me 'the pipeline guy', because I built most of our AI workflow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but overhyped, which is what I already tell people. At work I'd keep showing Sam the little time savers. Online I'd probably post something like 'told you, it's a good brush, not a painter'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools. But it'd mean my job's safe, my pay's good, and the agency keeps growing slowly. Honestly, with almost a year of savings and plenty of agencies nearby, I'd have nothing much to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and probably teach the other four at the agency the shortcuts I use. I'd keep my savings in the index fund and keep adding to it. I might start a small paid workshop for other designers on AI workflows, a couple of Saturdays a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored maybe. It's like finding out the new phone is just the old phone with a better camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at the agency lose out even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Joy, who does the resizing work by hand, because the routine stuff is the bit the tools already handle. I'd want to make sure she learns the tools too, not gets pushed out. Sam's decent, but he does watch costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards unions and public support. How does that sit with being the pipeline guy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see the tension. I think the tools should make our work better and our weeks shorter, not make us fewer. If I'm the one building the pipeline, I want a say in how the time saved gets used.

say: The tools are **useful but overhyped**: a good brush, not a painter.
I'd keep showing Sam **small time savers** at work.
think: My **job and pay** are safe and the agency keeps growing slowly.
With almost **a year** of savings and plenty of agencies nearby, I'm secure.
do: Teach the other four my **AI shortcuts** so nobody is left behind.
Keep adding to my **index fund** each month.
Run a paid **workshop** for designers on AI workflows a couple of Saturdays a year.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored**, like a new phone that's just the old one.
S0.quote: The tools should make our work better and our weeks shorter, not make us fewer.
fieldNote: Nikhil is the agency's **AI builder** and feels secure in the calm picture.
He worries for **Joy**, whose resizing work is the routine part tools already handle.
He holds a **tension** between enthusiasm for tools and his pro-worker views.

steps.text: Teach the four colleagues his AI shortcuts for ad resizing
Keep adding to his index fund every month
Run paid Saturday workshops on AI workflows for other designers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, it's real, and we need rules so the gains are shared. At the agency I'd push for training for everyone and no job cuts in the first year. Online I'd talk about a shorter working week as the fair way to share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of this fine, maybe better. I'm the one who runs the tools, so I'm the last person Sam lets go. The people I worry about are Joy and our copywriter, because their work is the kind the software eats first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd write down our whole workflow so anyone could run it, not just me. I'd push Sam to retrain Joy into checking and finishing the AI output instead of letting her go. I'd also put an extra few hundred a month into savings, just because the industry around us gets shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about other people. I'd feel a bit guilty, like I'm on the lifeboat and my friends are still in the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why write the workflow down? Doesn't that make you easier to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but hoarding it would make me the kind of person I don't want to be. If the agency survives because all five of us can use the tools, that's better than four people gone and me working seventy hours. I'd rather be useful than irreplaceable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good year after the change look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five of us still there, a four-day week, more clients because we're faster. Joy doing quality checks and art direction instead of resizing. That's the version I'd fight for.

say: AI is **here and real**, and we need rules so the gains are shared.
A **shorter week** is the fair way to share the time saved.
think: I'm the one who runs the tools, so I'm the **last one** Sam lets go.
**Joy** and our copywriter are the ones whose work goes first.
do: Write down our **whole workflow** in three months so anyone can run it.
Push Sam to **retrain Joy** into checking and finishing AI output.
Add a few **hundred a month** to savings as the industry gets shaky.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for others, and a bit **guilty** to be on the lifeboat.
S1.quote: I'd rather be useful than irreplaceable.
fieldNote: Nikhil expects his **own job** to be safe, which keeps him at uneasy.
He chooses **sharing knowledge** over hoarding it, against his own narrow interest.
His vision is concrete: **four-day week**, five staff kept, Joy moved to art direction.

steps.text: Write down the agency's full AI workflow within three months
Push Sam to retrain Joy as an AI output checker
Add a few hundred a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: wage support, a tax on the AI firms, and a pause on mass layoffs while people adjust. At work I'd be honest with the others that this changes everything. Online I'd be one of the loud ones, because I'd know what these tools can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job as it is ends within a couple of years of it arriving. If a machine can do almost any thinking work, it can also run the pipeline I built, so being the pipeline guy only buys me a year or two. There's no hands-on part of what I do, so the robot delay doesn't help me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd squeeze the most out of being early: take on extra freelance work setting up AI systems for other small agencies, and bank all of it. I'd move most of my index fund into something safer, because I wouldn't trust the markets in a shock like that. And I'd join a union branch, because when everyone's affected, groups matter more than individuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, because I've got money and I know the tools, but it's the first time I can't see what my job is in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning change for you, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's a short window where people like me are paid well to set things up, and then that window shuts. In two years I can't train into a whole new field, but I can earn and save hard while the window's open. The slower ones give me time to build something; this one only gives me time to bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya, your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya her testing job is probably in the same boat as mine, so we can't count on one of us carrying the other. We'd look at what we'd cut, which is mostly the flat with the nice view. And we'd talk about whether her parents' house outside the city makes more sense for a while.

say: We need **emergency rules**: wage support, a tax on AI firms and a layoff pause.
I'd be one of the **loud ones**, because I know what the tools can do.
think: My job **as it is** ends within a couple of years of AGI arriving.
With **no hands-on part** to my work, the robot delay gives me nothing.
do: Take **extra freelance work** setting up AI systems for other agencies, and bank it.
Move most of my **index fund** into something safer.

feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, because I have **money** and know the tools.
S2.quote: There's a short window where people like me are paid well to set things up, and then that window shuts.
fieldNote: Nikhil sees his early skill as a **short window**, not long-term safety.
He notes that his partner **Priya** works in testing, so both incomes are exposed.
He still feels **some control**, thanks to savings and skills.

steps.text: Take freelance jobs setting up AI systems for other small agencies
Move most of the index fund into safer savings
Join a designers' union branch in the first months
Consider moving into Priya's parents' house outside the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now, so let's start now. I'd push for the agency to become a co-op, owned by the five of us, so whatever the tools earn stays with us. Online I'd talk about public retraining money and a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the next three years are actually good for me, with lots of demand for people who can set up AI work. Then around 2031 the design job disappears, and I'm thirty-two, which is young enough to switch. So it's good money now and a big question later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd talk to Sam about the co-op idea and bank as much freelance setup money as I can. I'd start a part-time course in something that blends people and tech, maybe teaching design or digital skills, since teaching keeps a person in the room. And I'd keep investing, but more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a quieter way. It's a background hum, not an alarm, but I'd know my income has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if machines are going to do the work, the question is who owns the machines. If the five of us own the agency, the tools' earnings come back to us instead of to Sam's buyer. It's my politics turned into a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't teaching also thinking work that AI could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes. But kids and adults still need someone to show them, to notice when they're lost and to push them. I'd bet on the human part of teaching lasting longer than the human part of resizing ads.

The agency should become a **co-op** owned by the five of us.

Around **2031** my design job disappears, and I'm young enough to switch.

S3.quote: If machines are going to do the work, the question is who owns the machines.
fieldNote: Nikhil turns his **politics** into a practical plan: a worker-owned agency.
He sees a **boom then bust**: good money until 2031, then no design job.
He bets on **teaching** because the human part lasts longer.

steps.text: Pitch Sam on turning the agency into a staff-owned co-op

Start a part-time course to teach digital design skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, and wasting it would be a choice. I'd want governments to fund retraining now and set rules on who benefits. At the agency I'd say let's grow, but let's plan the exit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the next several years look good for me: more clients, better tools, and I'm the one who knows them. AGI in 2036 means my design work probably ends when I'm thirty-seven, but that's a long way off. I'd have time to build up savings and try two or three paths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep working, push my pay up because my AI skills are in demand, and save the extra. I'd start the co-op conversation slowly. And I'd take an evening course in teaching, just to see if I like it, with no pressure to finish quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. Ten years is like knowing you'll move cities: plenty of time to choose the neighbourhood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push your pay up. Isn't that at odds with sharing the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But if the agency is going to earn more from tools I set up, I'd rather some of it reaches staff, starting with me and Joy. I'd ask for raises for both of us at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not my next few years. More the long end, when the people with nothing saved hit 2036 at the same time. I'd want to be part of the group pushing for that support, not just looking after myself.

say: We've been given **a decade**, and wasting it would be a choice.
Governments should **fund retraining** now and set rules on who benefits.
think: The next **several years** look good, with more clients and better tools.
My design work probably ends at **thirty-seven**, but that's far away.
do: Ask for **raises** for me and Joy together, and save the extra.

S4.quote: Ten years is like knowing you'll move cities: plenty of time to choose the neighbourhood.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **own next years** look secure, so his worry is mostly about others.
He links his **raise** to Joy's, keeping his pro-worker views.
He treats the decade as time to **test paths**, not to rush.

steps.text: Ask Sam for raises for himself and Joy at the same time
Raise the co-op idea gradually with the other four
Take an evening course in teaching to test the fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole edge, knowing the tools early, only lasts a year or two there. What would help is wage support and a tax on the AI firms that pays for retraining. And laws that make it easier for small agencies to become co-ops, so workers own a piece of what replaces them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I feel responsible. I sometimes do. I built the pipeline that makes our agency need fewer people, hoping for shorter weeks, not fewer jobs. I'd want that on record.

headlineQuote: I built the pipeline that makes our agency need fewer people, hoping for shorter weeks, not fewer jobs.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** ad designer at a five-person agency for small web shops.
He uses AI **every day** and built the agency's workflow, which he openly shares.
He feels secure in the calm and steady pictures, but worries for **colleagues** like Joy.
In the AGI pictures he sees a **short window** of good money before his design work ends.
He wants **co-ops**, a shorter week and AI taxes to fund retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his early edge with the tools lasts only a year or two.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** and an AI tax that funds retraining.
Laws that help small agencies become **co-ops** owned by their staff.
